name: Uradhi
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/ 'person' ... /ukúmala/ 'sweet potato' /ayparúmpiwa/ 'sparrowhawk' (ii) In the case of words containing long vowels, it is always the long vowels that receive primary stress, regardless of their position in the word. (Note that it is possible to have a word that contains two primary stresses.)
new_statements.citation: Crowley, Terry. 1983. 'Uradhi', pp. 306-428 of R.M.W. Dixon & Barry J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages, Vol. 3. Canberra: ANU Press.
new_statements.locator: section 2.3 'Stress', p. 322 (PDF p. 344 of the ANU open-access volume)
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (lines 935-960) and the 150-dpi page image; also cross-checked the full ANU open-access volume held by the project (PDF p.344 = book p.322). Section 2.3 STRESS is exactly where the first reader says and the quoted passage is verbatim: 'The stress rules throughout the Uradhi dialects appear to be fairly uniform. The most important generalisations regarding stress are: (i) Primary stress is placed on the antepenultimate syllable, (i.e. third syllable from the end), of a word that contains only short vowels. Words of three syllables or less are therefore stressed on the initial syllable. Examples (from the Atampaya dialect): /áma/.. /ukúmala/.. /ayparúmpiwa/.. (ii) In the case of words…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In words with only short vowels, primary stress falls on the antepenultimate syllable (hence on the first syllable of mono-, di- and trisyllables); any long vowel attracts primary stress wherever it stands, so a word with two long vowels has two primary stresses (e.g. /t̪á:rá:namu/ 'reef-GEN', /amá:ka/ 'message stick').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress; only the note that a word with more than one long vowel can carry two primary stresses.
new_statements.exceptions: Long vowels override the antepenultimate rule (stressed regardless of position). No lexical exceptions listed. Rules said to be 'fairly uniform' across the three dialects (Atampaya, Angkamuthi, Yadhaykenu); examples are Atampaya.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated on phonemic (underlying) word forms in citation; note the language's extensive word-final sandhi (2.4.1) alters surface syllable count at utterance/word edges, which the stress section does not discuss.
new_statements.identity_note: urad1239 'Uradhi' is a retired/bookkeeping Glottolog languoid (ISO urf). Crowley 1983 uses 'Uradhi' as a cover name for a Northern Paman dialect chain and describes three dialects: Atampaya (Glottolog atam1239), Angkamuthi and Yadhaykenu; the stress examples are all Atampaya, and the rule is stated to hold across all three. The 2026-09-12 catalog already pins this same page (Crowley 1983:322) under key atam1239, so a urad1239 entry would duplicate that source; decide whether to key it once (atam1239) or alias urad1239 to it.
